analysis.one_liner: Charges opioid makers up to $2 billion a year for ten years to fund addiction treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a single cosponsor and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to collect an annual fee of up to $2 billion, split by each company's share of the opioid market, from drug manufacturers that made opioid painkillers since 1999. Opioids used to treat addiction, cancer, or hospice patients would be exempt. The money would go to the federal block grant that funds state substance-abuse prevention and treatment programs.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction and their communities, through an estimated $2 billion a year in new federal funding for state prevention and treatment programs, paid by the drug companies that sold the opioids rather than by taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would raise up to $2 billion per year for ten years from opioid manufacturers, with each company's fee set by its share of the opioid market since 1999 [S3].
All of the money would be transferred to the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment block grant, the main federal funding stream states use for addiction prevention and treatment services [S3].

Opioids used exclusively for addiction treatment (such as medications for opioid use disorder) and for cancer or hospice patients would be exempt, so the fee would not raise the cost of treatment itself [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers that produced opioid painkillers since 1999, in proportion to their share of that market, for ten years.

drawbacks.text: The fee is retroactive in spirit: it charges companies for opioids they lawfully manufactured going back decades, and manufacturers would likely argue that penalizing past lawful sales after the fact is unfair and would invite litigation that could delay or derail the funding [S3].

A fee on opioid products could be passed through to prices of remaining opioid medications, raising costs for pain patients who legitimately need them, though the exemption for cancer, hospice, and addiction-treatment drugs limits that [S3].

Tying new treatment money to a fee on a shrinking market creates a funding stream that depends on continued opioid sales and on HHS's judgment about market shares, which could be contested and unpredictable year to year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and targeted: roughly $2 billion a year of new money for state addiction treatment, drawn from the companies that profited from the opioid market rather than from general taxpayers. The main risks are legal challenge over charging companies for past lawful conduct and possible price pass-through to pain patients, but the exemptions for treatment, cancer, and hospice drugs and the block grant structure address the most serious objections. The cost falls on a concentrated industry with documented ties to the crisis; the benefit spreads broadly across communities hit by the epidemic.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on June 5, 2019 [S1].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to the Health Subcommittee on June 6, 2019 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill had zero cosponsors [S4] and the complete action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without coming to a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers are better off: they never faced the $2 billion annual fee, and no new dedicated treatment funding was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who never paid the fee

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a fee on opioid manufacturers to fund the substance abuse treatment block grant.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup in the 18 months remaining in the Congress.

against.name: House colleagues of both parties
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors during the bill's entire life.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote, and its only supporter was a single House Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have charged companies that made opioid painkillers since 1999 up to $2 billion a year, apportioned by market share, to fund addiction treatment. The industry avoided the fee entirely when the bill died without a vote.

Providers and state programs funded through the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment block grant would have received roughly $2 billion a year in new funding. They gain nothing because the bill never advanced.
